description_full: Hasbro, Inc. operates as a toy and game company in the United States, Europe, Canada, Mexico, Latin America, Australia, China, and Hong Kong. The company offers trading cards and collectibles, action figures, arts and crafts and creative play products, dolls, play sets, preschool toys, plush products, vehicles and toy-related specialty products, sports action products and accessories, and other consumer products; and licensed products, such as apparel, publishing products, home goods and electronics, and toy products. It also engages in the sourcing, marketing, and sale of toy and game products; and promotes its brands through the out-licensing of trademarks, characters, and other brand and intellectual property rights to third parties through the sale of branded consumer products, such as toys and apparel. In addition, the company is involved in the promotion of its brands through the development of trading cards, role-playing, and digital game experiences based on Hasbro and Wizards of the Coast games; and license certain brands to other third-party digital game developers who transform Hasbro brand-based characters and other intellectual properties, into digital gaming experiences. Further, it develops and produces of Hasbro-branded entertainment content, including film, television, children's programming, digital content, and live entertainment. The company sells its products to retailers, distributors, wholesalers, discount stores, specialty hobby stores, drug stores, mail order houses, catalog stores, department stores, and other traditional retailers, as well as ecommerce retailers under the MAGIC: THE GATHERING, MONOPOLY, HASBRO GAMES, PLAY-DOH, TRANSFORMERS, DUNGEONS & DRAGONS, NERF, and PEPPA PIG, as well as LUCASFILMS' STAR WARS, BEYBLADE, Final Fantasy, The Lord of the Rings, Fallout, SPIDER-MAN, and THE AVENGERS brands. Hasbro, Inc. was founded in 1923 and is headquartered in Pawtucket, Rhode Island.

financial_summary: Hasbro, Inc. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $16.9B market cap on $5.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The business throws off $830M in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 22.3× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.1× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.0× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 26% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.87, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.18 vs 5y 0.83), so read it loosely.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $99.64 (margin of safety -21%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 63%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $60.30 to $162 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.95).
It converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9 and cash conversion of only -2.77x.

hlth: Leverage is heavy at 22.3x net debt to EBITDA ($1.4B of cash against $3.3B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 0.1x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -2.9% over 3 years, -0.4% over 5 years and 10.5% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 39%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -0.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.18 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 18% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 115%.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (1.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 14, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (14 sales, net $8.1M sold).
It returns 2.3% a year to shareholders (2.3% in dividends).
